m: This is the ritual direction for the middle narrative. The seer is Vishnu, the deity Shri Mahalakshmi, the metre ushnik, the power Shakambhari, the seed Durga, the element air, and the form the Yajurveda. It is recited to please Shri Mahalakshmi. The meditation begins: she holds a rosary, a blood-red axe, a mace, arrows, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, a spear, a sword, a shield, a water-lily, a bell, a vessel of wine, a trident, a noose, and the discus, and she shines like coral.
I serve here Mahalakshmi, seated on a lotus, crusher of the buffalo. Om Hrim. The seer said:
Long ago there was a war between the gods and the asuras that lasted a full hundred years, when Mahisha was lord of the asuras and Purandara was lord of the gods.
There the army of the gods was defeated by asuras of great valour. Having conquered all the gods, Mahishasura became Indra.
Then the defeated gods, placing the lotus-born lord of creatures at their head, went to where Shiva and Vishnu, whose banner is Garuda, were.
The gods told the two of them what had happened, the doings of Mahishasura, and the full account of the gods' defeat.
He himself has taken over the offices of the sun, Indra, Agni, Vayu, the moon, Yama, Varuna, and the others.
Cast out of heaven by that evil-minded Mahisha, all the hosts of gods wander on the earth like mortals.
All this activity of the enemy of the immortals has been told to you. We have come to you for refuge. Please think how he may be slain.
Hearing the gods' words in this way, Madhusudana and Shambhu grew angry, their faces bent with frowns.
Then a great splendour came forth from the face of the discus-bearer, who was filled with extreme anger, and from Brahma and from Shankara.
A very great splendour also came forth from the bodies of the other gods, beginning with Shakra, and all of it came together into one.
The gods saw there a peak of exceedingly intense splendour, blazing like a mountain, the quarters filled with its flames.
That unequalled splendour, born from the bodies of all the gods and gathered in one place, became a woman, her lustre pervading the three worlds.
What had been Shambhu's splendour became her face. Her hair came from Yama's, and her arms from Vishnu's splendour.
The pair of her breasts came from the moon's, and her waist from Indra's. Her shanks and thighs came from Varuna's, and her hips from the earth's splendour.
Her feet came from Brahma's splendour, her toes from the sun's, the fingers of her hands from the Vasus, and her nose from Kubera's.
Her teeth arose from Prajapati's splendour, and her three eyes were born from the fire's splendour.
Her eyebrows came from the splendour of the two twilights, and her ears from the wind's. The auspicious Goddess arose from the splendours of the other gods as well.
Seeing her, born from the mass of splendour of all the gods, the immortals who had been oppressed by Mahisha rejoiced. Then the gods gave her their own weapons.
The bearer of the Pinaka drew a trident from his own trident and gave it to her. Krishna, drawing a discus from his own discus, gave that.
Varuna gave a conch, and the fire gave a spear. The wind gave a bow and two quivers filled with arrows.
Indra, the thousand-eyed lord of the immortals, drew a thunderbolt from his own thunderbolt and gave it to her, and a bell from the elephant Airavata.
Yama gave a staff from his staff of death, and the lord of the waters gave a noose. Prajapati gave a rosary, and Brahma a water-pot.
The sun placed his own rays in every pore of her hair. Time gave her a sword and a spotless shield.
The ocean of milk gave a pure necklace and a pair of unaging garments, and also a divine crest-jewel, earrings, and bracelets.
It gave a bright half-moon, armlets on all her arms, a pair of spotless anklets, and an unsurpassed neck-ornament.
It gave jewelled rings on all her fingers. Vishvakarman gave her a very bright axe,
weapons of many forms, and armour that could not be pierced, a garland of unwithering lotuses on her head, and another on her breast.
The ocean gave her a very beautiful lotus. Himavan gave a lion as her mount, and jewels of many kinds.
The lord of wealth gave a drinking-cup filled with wine. Shesha, lord of all serpents, who bears this earth,
gave her a serpent-necklace adorned with a great jewel. The other gods too honoured the Goddess with ornaments and weapons.
Honoured, she roared aloud, laughing loudly again and again. The whole sky was filled by her dreadful roar.
From that boundless, immense roar a great echo arose. All the worlds were shaken, and the oceans trembled.
The earth shook, and all the mountains moved. The gods, with joy, cried Victory to her whose mount is the lion.
The sages praised her, their bodies bent in devotion. Seeing the whole triple world thrown into turmoil, the enemies of the immortals
rose up, all their armies arrayed, weapons raised. What is this? cried Mahishasura in anger,
and he rushed toward that sound, surrounded by all the asuras. Then he saw the Goddess, her lustre pervading the three worlds,
the earth bent under the tread of her foot, the sky scraped by her crown, all the nether worlds stirred, and she herself sounding with the twang of her bowstring.
She stood filling the directions on every side with a thousand arms. Then a battle began between the Goddess and the enemies of the gods.
The quarters were lit up by the many weapons and missiles that were released. Chikshura, a great asura, general of Mahishasura's army,
fought, and Chamara fought with others, attended by a fourfold army. The great asura named Udagra fought with six myriads of chariots.
Mahahanu fought with a thousand myriads, and the great asura Asiloma with fifty million.
Bashkala fought in the battle with six hundred myriads. Surrounded by many floods of elephants and horses,
and surrounded by a crore of chariots, he fought in that battle. Bidala, surrounded by fifty myriads and by myriads of chariots,
fought in the encounter there. And other great asuras, surrounded by chariots, elephants, and horses in the tens of thousands,
fought the Goddess there in battle. Mahishasura himself was there in the fight, surrounded by crores upon crores of thousands of chariots, of elephants,
and of horses. They fought the Goddess in battle with lances, with bhindipala darts, with spears, and with maces,
and with swords, axes, and pattisha weapons. Some hurled spears, some nooses, and others
set out to kill the Goddess with sword-blows. Chandika, the Goddess, raining her own weapons and missiles,
cut all those weapons and missiles as if in play. Her face unstrained, praised by the gods and the seers,
the sovereign released weapons and missiles into the bodies of the asuras. Her mount, the maned lion, also grew angry, shook his mane,
and moved among the asura armies like a fire through forests. The breaths that Ambika breathed out as she fought in battle
at once became hosts, in hundreds of thousands. Strengthened by the Goddess's power, they fought with axes, bhindipala darts, swords, and pattishas,
destroying the bands of asuras. Some hosts beat drums, and others blew conches,
and still others played mridangas in that great festival of battle. Then the Goddess, with trident, mace, showers of spears,
and swords and other weapons, slew great asuras by the hundred. She also felled others who had been bewildered by the sound of her bell.
She bound some asuras with a noose and dragged them along the ground. Some were cut in two by sharp sword-strokes, and others,
crushed by the fall of the mace, lay on the earth. Some, struck hard by the pestle, vomited blood.
Some fell to the ground, their chests split by the trident. Some were made into an unbroken mass by the flood of arrows on the battlefield.
Those tormentors of the gods gave up their lives, looking like hawks. The arms of some were cut off, and the necks of others were cut.
The heads of others fell, and others were torn open at the waist. Other great asuras fell to the earth with their thighs cut away.
Some were left by the Goddess with one arm, one eye, or one foot, cut in two. Others, even with their heads cut off, fell and rose again.
Headless trunks fought the Goddess, grasping excellent weapons. Others danced there in the battle, keeping time with the music.
The headless trunks, their heads severed, had swords, spears, and lances in their hands. Other great asuras called to the Goddess, Stand, stand!
The earth became impassable there, where that great battle was, with fallen chariots, elephants, horses, and asuras.
Great rivers of blood soon flowed there, in the midst of the asura army, among the elephants, asuras, and horses.
In a moment Ambika brought that great army of asuras to destruction, as a fire consumes a great heap of straw and wood.
And the lion, sending forth a great roar and shaking his mane, sought out the lives from the bodies of the enemies of the immortals.
The battle that the Goddess's hosts fought there with the asuras was such that the gods were pleased, and they released a rain of flowers in the sky.
